notes.text: I saw — In a vision. The Lord - The Divine Majesty as he subsisteth in three persons. His train - His royal and judicial robe; for he is represented as a judge.

Stood — As ministers attending upon their Lord. Seraphim - An order of holy angels, thus called from fire and burning, which this word properly signifies; to represent either their nature, which is bright and glorious, subtile, and pure; or their property, of fervent zeal for God's service and glory. Covered - Out of profound reverence.

Cried — Singing in consort. Holy - This is repeated thrice, to intimate the Trinity of persons united in the Divine essence. Glory - Of the effects and demonstrations of his glorious holiness, as well as of his power, wisdom, and goodness.
The posts — Together with the door itself. Such violent motions were commonly tokens of God's anger. Smoak - Which elsewhere is a token of God's presence and acceptance, but here of his anger.

l am — I am a great sinner, as many other ways, so particularly by my lips. I am an unclean branch of an unclean tree; besides my own uncleanness, I have both by my omissions and commissions involved myself in the guilt of their sins. Have seen - The sight of this glorious and holy God gives me cause to fear that he is come to judgment against me.
Flew — By God's command. A coal - Both a token and an instrument of purification. The altar - Of burnt-offering.
Laid it — So as only to touch my lips, and not to burn them; which God could easily effect. Lo - This is a sign that I have pardoned and purged the uncleanness of thy lips.

Who — To deliver the following message. The change of the number, I and us, is very remarkable; and both being meant of one and the same Lord, do sufficiently intimate a plurality of persons in the Godhead.

Perceive not — The Hebrew words are imperative; yet they are not to be taken as a command what the people ought to do, but only as a prediction what they would do. The sense is, because you have so long heard my words, and seen my works, to no purpose, and have hardened your hearts, and will not learn nor reform, I will punish you in your own kind, your sin shall be your punishment. I will still continue my word and works to you, but will withdraw my Spirit, so that you shall be as unable, as now you are unwilling, to understand.

Fat — Stupid and senseless. This making of their hearts fat, is here ascribed to the prophet, as it is ascribed to God in the repetition of this prophecy, John xii, 40, because God inflicted this judgment upon them by the ministry of the prophet, partly by way of prediction, foretelling that this would be the effect of his preaching; and partly by withdrawing the light and help of his Spirit. Heavy - Make them dull of hearing. Lest - That they may not be able, as before they were not willing to see. Convert - Turn to God.

Lord — An abrupt speech, arising from the prophet's great passion and astonishment: how long shall this dreadful judgment last? Until - Until this land be totally destroyed, first by the Babylonians, and afterward by the Romans.
Removed — Hath caused this people to be carried away captive into far countries. A forsaking - 'Till houses and lands be generally forsaken of their owners.

A tenth — A small remnant reserved, that number being put indefinitely. Return - Out of the Babylonish captivity, into their own land. Eaten - That remnant shall be devoured a second time, by the kings of Syria, and afterwards by the Romans. Yet - Yet there shall be another remnant, not such an one as that which came out of Babylon, but an holy seed, who shall afterwards look upon him whom they have pierced, and mourn over him. When - Who when their leaves are cast in winter, have a substance within themselves, a vital principle, which preserves life in the root of the tree, and in due time sends it forth into all the branches. The support - Of the land or people, which, were it not for the sake of these, should be finally rooted out. Ahaz afraid of Rezin and Pekah, is comforted by Isaiah, ver. 1-9. Refusing to chuse a sign, Christ is promised for one, ver. 10- 16. His judgment should come by Assyria, ver. 17-25.

glossa.text:
*In the year,* etc. ((HIER.)) Ozias himself is Azarias, etc., *as far as* falling upon his face, he cries out with a loud voice to the Lord.

 *King Ozias.* The king, namely the leper, who usurped the priesthood.

*I saw the Lord.* Christ, namely. The Son was seen in the habit of one reigning; the Holy Spirit spoke, because of the fellowship of majesty and the unity of substance.

*Upon a throne high,* etc. ((HIER.)) He who sees the Lord reigning in the heavenly powers sees him upon a throne high and lifted up, which are the Thrones and the Dominations, etc.

Some say that the seraphim are powers in heaven attending upon God and praising him, which are sent upon ministries chiefly to those who have need of purgation, and, for certain sins, in part to punishments.

((ID.)) Cherubim, a multitude of knowledge, upon whom the Lord is shown to sit after the manner of a charioteer, whence: *Thou that sittest upon the cherubim,* etc. But the seraphim, apart from this place, I do not remember to have read in the canonical Scriptures. They err therefore who are wont to write in their prayers: Thou that sittest upon the cherubim and seraphim.

*They stood.* ((ID.)) That is, they stand attending upon God; they fly, showing forth God; they lay bare as it were the middle part; they do not make manifest the things that are veiled; they do not veil the things that are known.

*Six wings to one.* ((ID.)) Victorinus understands the twelve apostles. But we, the twelve stones of the altar which iron did not touch, and the twelve gems in the diadem of the priest.

((ID.)) The angels are said to have wings, because they dwell in the higher places, or because of their swift running to and fro in all things, as the winds also are called winged.

*With two they veiled his face.* What things were before these I know not, etc., *as far as* the angels also and the preachers teach nothing thereof; likewise:

*They veiled the feet.* ((HIER.)) What is to be after this world we know not: the middle things, however, which were made in six days or ages, or are made; we know only *With two they veiled,* because we have knowledge of the present alone.

((ID.)) My Hebrew has entered by a far other way, etc., *as far as* and then, being truly purged in the lips, I said to the Lord: *Behold I, send me.*

*And they cried.* ((ID.)) They do not say it lightly, but pronounce with a cry a confession salutary for all: Holy, holy, holy, because they themselves also, namely the seraphim, are holy: for nothing is holier than these: but they marvel that the Son so humbled himself and underwent the cross, and became known to earthly things.

*Holy, holy,* etc. The mystery of the Trinity. In both Testaments the Trinity is preached, the Lord Christ, namely, who here is of four letters, which is set down properly of God: Iod, He, Iod, He; that is, two *ia,* which doubled make the ineffable name of God.

*The whole earth is full.* ((ID.)) And it shall be filled, etc., *as far as* after two and forty years from the passion of the Lord.
*The lintels.* In the Old Testament the Lord spoke, etc., *as far as* which taking up we say: *We know in part, and we prophesy in part ((I Cor. XIII))*.

*Polluted.* ((ID.)) This he says because of the fellowship of the people, with whom he was constrained to speak. It is harmful to live with sinners.

*I dwell.* Note that one must not tarry with sinners.

*And I have seen with my eyes the King, the Lord of hosts: and one flew to me.* So Abraham, after he had seen the Lord and heard his voice, confesses himself to be ashes and dust, because however great the dignity of men may be, it grows cheap in comparison of him.

*Of the seraphim.* ((ID.)) Seraphim with *m* we say in the masculine gender, with *n* in the neuter gender plural. Seraphim, however, can be said in the singular, as cherubim and cherub.

*And in his hand.* That is, by his working, that is, of Christ. The coal, that is, charity, which with the tongs, that is, the teaching of the two Testaments, he had taken from the altar, and had set before Isaias for an example.

*A coal.* ((ID.)) The Seventy: a carbuncle, a fiery stone, which because of its flame-like colour is called igneous.

*With tongs.* ((ID.)) This is the ladder of Jacob, the sword twice sharpened, etc., *as far as* comprehending the word of God with the double edge of the precepts.

*From the altar.* Which John saw in the Apocalypse, which is full of fiery coals, wherewith sins can be purged.

*Behold I have touched thy lips:* whence: *What may be given to thee, or what may be added to thee for a deceitful tongue? The sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals that lay waste ((Psal. CXIX))*. This is the word of God, of which it is said: Thou hast coals of fire, thou shalt sit upon them, these shall be to thee for a help.

*And the iniquity shall be taken away.* ((ID.)) Jeremias, who was a boy, and therefore almost free from sin, is purged by the touch of a hand alone. But to Isaias, who says: I am a man polluted in the lips, an angel is sent with a coal.

*Whom shall I send?* He does not compel, but seeks the will: for the will alone deserves the reward. But Isaias, as one purged, offers himself of his own accord.

*Send me.* ((ID.)) He thinks that he is to announce good, etc., *as far as* that it was not of rashness but of obedience that he offered himself.

*Hear ye that hear.* ((ID.)) Luke according to the Seventy in the Acts of the Apostles: *With the ear you shall hear, and shall not understand,* etc., *as far as* and he uses Greek testimonies rather than Hebrew.

*Blind,* etc. ((ID.)) To which is like, etc., *as far as* nor is it cruelty of God, but mercy, the unbelieving being blinded, to enlighten the humble.

*And he be converted.* Although the sin be grievous, if anyone be converted, he can be saved: but these, for the greatness of their crime, are unworthy of penance.

*And still.* And in place of, that is, still out of that nation a tithing, as if still a tenth part of that nation shall remain.

*And it shall be.* Under Hadrian Judaea was laid waste again, in the fiftieth year indeed after the captivity of the Romans. For they were forbidden by public laws to enter Judaea.

notes.text: The gods — Before kings and princes.
Temple — Where the ark was. He was not permitted to enter into it. Magnified - For thou hast glorified thy word or promise unto me more than any other of thy glorious perfections.
The kings — A prophecy of the calling of the Gentiles. Hear - The gospel preached among then.
The ways — His wonderful counsel and gracious providences.

Perfect — Will finish the great work of my deliverance. Forsake not - Or, do not give over, the work of my salvation, which is thus far advanced, not by any human help, but by thy power and providence. This psalm is, by many of the Jewish doctors, esteemed the most excellent in the whole book. The omniscience of God is here asserted, ver. 1-6. Proved by two arguments; That he is everywhere present, ver. 7-12. And that he made us, ver. 13-16. This may fill us with pleasing admiration of God, ver. 17, 18. With an holy hatred of sin, ver. 19-22. And with an holy satisfaction in our own integrity, ver. 23, 24. To the chief musician, A psalm of David.

glossa.text:
*A psalm to David himself.* ((CASS.)) The captive, who had wept, as though Jerusalem and the temple were rebuilt, and as a fellow-citizen with that part of Jerusalem which was not captive, that is, with the angels, rejoices and praises first the benefits given him. In the person therefore of the Church, which is in the things above in hope, awaiting to be there in reality, he says, *I will confess.*

*I will confess to thee, O Lord.* First, he commends the benefits given him: secondly, he tells how these are spread abroad unto all, there, *Let them confess to thee, O Lord,* etc. *In the sight.* ((AUG.)) In praising I set before myself the angels, to whom I look to be made equal in dignity hereafter, as I am now. But these in the praise of God set before themselves nothing else but himself. *In the sight* therefore *of the angels,* in that purity wherein the angels behold thee, that in thee alone they may rest, I *will sing to thee.*

*For thy mercy.* ((ID.)) *All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth:* There are no other ways by which he came to us, there are no others by which we may come to him: let us render these to God, mercy in succouring, truth in judging. *Above every holy name of thine.* ((CASS.)) Or above thy holy name, when thy worship became known to us.
*In the soul.* And because in the soul a carnal multiplication can take place, he adds, *strength,* as though: I seek nothing else in the soul but strength.

*Let them confess.* ((ID.)) The second part, where it is said *dici*; read *dicit*, "he tells" how these good things are to be spread abroad unto all. As it were, after my example: *Let them confess,* etc. *All the words of thy mouth.* ((AUG.)) Which have now been revealed everywhere, and sent unto all nations, etc., *as far as* and thus, the fleece being dried, *they heard all the words,* etc.

*Great is the glory.* ((ID.)) If they are humble, they love and sing this; for if they exalt themselves, let them fear what follows. *For the Lord is high. He looketh on the low things.* ((CASS.)) Here is not the human condition, where the humble man is despised and the proud man regarded; but the Lord regards the humble.

*The high he knoweth afar off.* ((AUG.)) The proud man does not this, etc., *as far as* mourning this sojourning, whence it is subjoined.

*If I shall walk in the midst of tribulation.* Otherwise he does not quicken, save *in the midst of tribulation,* whence, *Blessed are they that mourn, woe to them that laugh.*

*Upon the wrath.* ((ID.)) This very thing, that they are angry with me, is thy chastisement upon them, that is, thy punishment. For to be angry is to them a punishment, not *noc* only a fault. While therefore thou permittest this, thou stretchest forth the hand of vengeance upon them all.

*Thy right hand.* God has not a right hand or a left, but the right hand of God is called eternal happiness, the left, temporal happiness. Sometimes therefore he does not save his saints in the left hand, but he always saves them in the right.
*He will repay.* ((AUG.)) What I cannot do, etc., *as far as* in whom the princes of the world found no sin, wherefore they should kill him.

notes.text: Ye are saved, if ye hold fast — Your salvation is begun, and will be perfected, if ye continue in the faith. Unless ye have believed in vain - Unless indeed your faith was only a delusion.
I received — From Christ himself. It was not a fiction of my own. Isaiah liii, 8, 9.
According to the scriptures — He proves it first from scripture, then from the testimony of a cloud of witnesses. Psalm xvi, 10.
By the twelve — This was their standing appellation; but their full number was not then present.
Above five hundred — Probably in Galilee. A glorious and incontestable proof! The greater part remain - Alive.

Then by all the apostles — The twelve were mentioned ver. 5. This title here, therefore, seems to include the seventy; if not all those, likewise, whom God afterwards sent to plant the gospel in heathen nations.

An untimely birth — It was impossible to abase himself more than he does by this single appellation. As an abortion is not worthy the name of a man, so he affirms himself to be not worthy the name of an apostle.
I persecuted the church — True believers are humbled all their lives, even for the sins they committed before they believed.

I laboured more than they all — That is, more than any of them, from a deep sense of the peculiar love God had shown me. Yet, to speak more properly, it is not I, but the grace of God that is with me - This it is which at first qualified me for the work, and still excites me to zeal and diligence in it.
Whether I or they, so we preach — All of us speak the same thing.

glossa.text: *By which also you are saved.* If you hold fast that Gospel, that is, the resurrection of the dead, on the ground on which I confirmed it to you, that is, by the resurrection of Christ. *Unless you have believed in vain.* Which is, if you do not hold the resurrection of the dead. That faith is empty which is not received under the hope of resurrection.

*He rose again the third day.* And this I said according to the Scriptures. For Osee says: *After two days he will quicken us, and on the third day we shall rise again in his sight ((Ose. VI))*. If he who was dead and buried rose again, doubt not that the dead and the buried shall rise again.
*He was seen by Cephas.* Before the other men to whom he is read to have appeared in the Gospel, otherwise it would be contrary to that which is read, that he appeared first to the women.

*As one born out of due time.* He is called one born out of due time because he was born outside the lawful season, that is, before he ought, or because, born again later and more tardily, he received the apostolate when Christ had already been taken up. Or, like one born out of due time, because I am the least, whether in time and calling, not in dignity, in labour, or in preaching. This he said truly, for humility's sake, and he proves it, saying: *I am not worthy.* Why then an Apostle? *But by the grace of God* At the first, grace alone, since no merits went before save evil ones. But afterwards, through grace, merits begin.

*More abundantly.* This was the more fulfilled, because he lived by the work of his hands, and did no less for the Gospel. And lest the will without the grace of God should be thought able to do anything, he adds: *Not I, but the grace,* etc
*And so you believed.* He reproves them: because, though this faith was manifest among all the churches, they nevertheless had fallen away from it.

notes.text: Matt. iv, 18; Mark i, 16.
Their net brake — Began to tear.
Depart from me, for I am a sinful man — And therefore not worthy to be in thy presence.
They forsook all and followed him — They had followed him before, John i, 43, but not so as to forsake all. Till now, they wrought at their ordinary calling.

glossa.text:
*And it came to pass.* Neither by time nor by place is the crowd restrained from its zeal for being healed; evening presses on, and yet it follows; the lake meets them, and the crowd presses, and therefore he went up into Peter's ship.

*He stood beside. ((BEDA.))* The lake signifies the present world. But the Lord is now no longer in the lake, as being now no longer in passible flesh, but beside the lake, because in that flesh in which he suffered he came to the stability of perpetual rest.

*He saw two ships. ((ID.))* The two ships, mystically, signify the circumcision and the uncircumcision, which he saw, because in each people *he knoweth who are his,* whose hearts comes forth from the waves of the world to the tranquillity of the life to come, as it were to the shore, by living mercifully.
*He asked him. ((ID.))* That he first asks the ship to be drawn back a little from the land, etc., *as far as* it pertains to the more remote Gentiles to whom it was afterwards preached.

*Launch out into the deep. ((AMBR.))* Although it is commanded to others that they let down their nets, etc., *as far as* or the Church is instructed and armed from the flowing gifts of the Holy Ghost.
*At thy word,* etc. ((BEDA.)) Unless by the word of grace the instruments of disputations have been let down, etc., *as far as* even amid the scandals of persecutors.
*And they filled. ((ID.))* This filling grows even unto the end of the world, etc., *as far as* and such humility deserves the merciful consolation of the Lord.

*From henceforth. ((ID.))* This pertains specially to Peter himself, to whom is expounded what the catch of fishes signifies. But as then he took fishes by nets, so at some time he shall take men by words, wherein Peter is a type of the whole Church.

echoes.text: But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: Paul's creedal 'Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures' (v.3) draws on the Servant who is 'wounded for our transgressions' and on whom the LORD lays 'the iniquity of us all.' Volume is moderate (no verbatim quotation) but coherence is high: the vicarious sin-bearing death is the only OT text supplying the formula, and Isaiah 53 was a primary resurrection-era proof-text. Availability is secure.

echoes.text: He was taken away by oppression and judgment; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living and stricken for the disobedience of my people? They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death; although he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth. Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his […]
echoes.note: The Servant 'cut off out of the land of the living,' 'numbered with the transgressors,' who 'bore the sin of many,' and is afterward vindicated ('he shall see... he shall prolong his days') undergirds the death-burial-vindication shape of the kerygma in vv.3-5. Recurrence: Paul appeals to Isaiah 53 elsewhere (Rom 4:25; 10:16). The 'according to the Scriptures' refrain points here for the death.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up' is the strongest single OT candidate for 'raised on the third day according to the Scriptures' (v.4), since no other text gives a third-day resurrection. Targumic/rabbinic tradition read Hosea 6:2 of resurrection, supporting availability. Contested because Paul never cites it explicitly and the LXX wording differs.

echoes.text: For you will not leave my soul in Sheol, neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption.
echoes.note: 'You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, nor let your holy one see corruption' was the apostolic resurrection proof-text (Acts 2:27; 13:35) and plausibly stands behind 'raised on the third day according to the Scriptures.' Coherence with the burial-then-raising sequence (vv.4) is good; volume is low here since Paul does not quote it. Marked echo, not quotation.

echoes.text: Yahweh prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.
echoes.note: 'Three days and three nights in the belly of the fish' is a possible scriptural warrant for the third-day timing, read figurally of death and deliverance (cf. Matt 12:40). Volume and recurrence in Paul are nil, so this is a faint, contested figural reading offered only because the 'according to the Scriptures' for the third day demands OT grounding.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Then I said, “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips: for my eyes have seen the King, Yahweh of Armies!”
echoes.note: Peter's reaction, falling at Jesus' knees and crying 'Depart from me, for I am a sinful man,' replays the prophet's response to theophany: confrontation with the holy provokes confession of uncleanness ('Woe is me, for I am a man of unclean lips'). Both join recognition of divine presence to commissioning ('Don't be afraid... you will be catching people'). High volume and coherence with the call-narrative form.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send for many fishermen, says Yahweh, and they shall fish them up; and afterward I will send for many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain, and from every hill, and out of the clefts of the rocks.
echoes.note: The 'catching people alive' commission draws on the prophetic image of God sending fishermen to gather Israel ('I will send for many fishers, and they shall fish them'). The shared metaphor of human fishers as agents of God's ingathering gives volume; the call setting supplies coherence, though Jeremiah's image is originally one of judgment.

echoes.text: It shall happen, that every living creature which swarms, in every place where the rivers come, shall live; and there shall be a very great multitude of fish; for these waters have come there, and the waters of the sea shall be healed, and everything shall live wherever the river comes. It shall happen, that fishermen shall stand by it: from En Gedi even to En Eglaim shall be a place for the spreading of nets; their fish shall be after their kinds, as the […]
echoes.note: Ezekiel's temple-river vision teems with fish and stations fishers from Engedi to Eneglaim, a figure of eschatological abundance and life flowing outward. The miraculous superabundant catch may echo this image of overflowing life as a sign of the new creation, though the verbal links are faint.

echoes.text: and make men like the fish of the sea, like the creeping things, that have no ruler over them? He takes up all of them with the hook. He catches them in his net, and gathers them in his dragnet. Therefore he rejoices and is glad.
echoes.note: Habakkuk likens people gathered by the conqueror to fish caught in a net and hauled up. The fishers-of-men motif may invert this image of catching for destruction into one of catching for life. Faint and contested; offered for the recurrence of the fish-net-people complex in the prophets.

echoes.text: Abraham answered, “See now, I have taken it on myself to speak to the Lord, who am but dust and ashes.
echoes.note: Abraham's self-deprecation before the LORD ('I am but dust and ashes') models the creature's recognition of unworthiness in the divine presence, paralleling Peter's 'I am a sinful man.' The motif of the human cowering before manifest holiness is widely attested; low volume here.

echoes.text: Gideon saw that he was Yahweh’s angel; and Gideon said, “Alas, Lord Yahweh! Because I have seen Yahweh’s angel face to face!” Yahweh said to him, “Peace be to you! Don’t be afraid. You shall not die.”
echoes.note: Gideon's fear at having seen the angel of the LORD face to face, answered by 'Peace, do not fear,' parallels the theophanic-fear-and-reassurance pattern (Jesus' 'Don't be afraid'). The form is recurrent across call narratives, lending coherence though the link to Luke 5 is general.

Here am I, Lord; send me.

Here am I, Lord; send me.

Here am I, Lord; send me.
The nets break with abundance; the unworthy are called; do not be afraid.
Here am I, Lord; send me!
